strengths: Provides the first rigorous non-asymptotic complexity analysis for annealed importance sampling (AIS) and Jarzynski equality (JE) without assuming log-concavity or other isoperimetric conditions on the target, significantly generalizing prior work (Brosse et al. 2018, Ge et al. 2020) that relied on such assumptions.

Introduces a novel and elegant proof strategy connecting the complexity of normalizing constant estimation to the Wasserstein action of the interpolating curve, via Girsanov's theorem and optimal transport metric derivatives; this framework unifies continuous (ALD) and discretized (AIS) analyses in a conceptually clean way.

Derives concrete, interpretable complexity bounds (e.g., Thm. 6, Thm. 8) with explicit dependence on smoothness, dimension, and action, and connects these to physical concepts (dissipated work, stochastic thermodynamics), enriching the theoretical narrative.

Identifies and rigorously proves (Prop. 9) a fundamental limitation of the standard geometric interpolation curve (exponential action for a simple Gaussian mixture), motivating a well-justified new algorithm based on reverse diffusion samplers with favorable action bounds (Prop. 10) and a full framework for analyzing its complexity (Thm. 11).

Extremely thorough and self-contained technical exposition, including detailed appendices covering Girsanov/Nelson relations, thermodynamic integration analysis, variance bounds, and discussion connecting to related learning-based samplers (PIS, CMCD), showing broad awareness of and engagement with the literature.

Clarifies subtle but important relationships (e.g., equivalence of complexity for estimating Z vs. F, relation of the proposed criterion to bias/variance, TI as a special case of AIS), improving conceptual clarity of the field.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation; it remains unclear how tight the derived upper bounds are in practice or whether the proposed RDS-based algorithm outperforms AIS on realistic problems.

The complexity bounds are only upper bounds; the paper explicitly acknowledges that matching lower bounds are missing, so it is unclear whether the action-dependent rates are unavoidable or an artifact of the proof technique.

Assumption 2 (existence of a near-origin stationary point with R ≲ 1/√β and finite second moment) and the restriction to the geometric interpolation curve in Thm. 8 limit generality somewhat, and the annealing schedule parameter r's role/impact on the bound is not deeply explored beyond an illustrative example.

Section 6 (RDS) is more of a conceptual framework than a fully worked-out complexity theorem: the final complexity depends on existing (and quite heterogeneous, sometimes exponential-in-dimension) RDS score-estimation results, so no clean, novel end-to-end complexity guarantee analogous to Thm. 8 is obtained for the proposed algorithm.

The manuscript is very dense and notation-heavy, which may hinder accessibility for a broader ML audience despite being rigorous; the main text relies heavily on referring to lengthy appendices for essentially all proofs.

The practical significance of the specific oracle-complexity rates (e.g., epsilon^-4 dependence) relative to existing heuristics is not empirically or numerically benchmarked, making it hard to gauge real-world impact beyond the theoretical contribution.

strengths: Provides the first non-asymptotic complexity analysis of annealed importance sampling (AIS) without assuming log-concavity or isoperimetric conditions on the target, extending prior work (e.g., Brosse et al., Ge et al.) that relied on such assumptions.

The proof technique connecting Girsanov's theorem, optimal transport metric derivatives, and the 'action' of an interpolating curve is elegant and gives a unifying lens for analyzing Jarzynski equality, AIS, and reverse diffusion samplers within one framework.

The paper identifies a concrete failure mode of the widely-used geometric interpolation curve (exponential lower bound on action for a simple 1D Gaussian mixture, Prop. 9), motivating the proposed reverse-diffusion-based alternative and giving a principled explanation for known practical difficulties of AIS on multimodal targets.

Extensive and careful supplementary material (appendices) with full proofs, discussion of related equilibrium/non-equilibrium methods, connections to stochastic thermodynamics (Crooks fluctuation theorem, dissipated work), and additional results (e.g., variance bound, TV bound along OU process).
Good scholarship: thorough literature review distinguishing prior asymptotic/variance-based analyses from this non-asymptotic contribution.
weaknesses: The paper is entirely theoretical with no empirical validation whatsoever—none of the derived complexity bounds (Thm. 6, 8, 11) are illustrated or verified on even toy numerical experiments, making it hard to assess whether the bounds are practically meaningful, tight, or merely qualitative.

The central complexity bounds depend on the 'action' A of the interpolating curve, which is generally unknown/uncomputable in advance for a general non-log-concave target; the paper itself shows (Prop. 9) that A can be exponentially large for a simple Gaussian mixture, undermining the practical utility of the headline complexity result for AIS in exactly the non-log-concave setting the paper claims to address.

Section 6 (the proposed RDS-based algorithm), which is advertised as a key contribution to fix AIS's shortcomings, does not deliver a self-contained complexity bound: Theorem 11 only reduces the guarantee to controlling KL(Q||Q†), and the actual complexity 'framework' just imports existing (and often extremely poor, e.g., exponential-in-1/ε) results on score-based samplers from other papers (App. E.5), so the promised improvement over AIS is not clearly established.

Assumption 2 requiring the stationary point norm R ≲ 1/√β is restrictive and its necessity/generality is not well justified beyond 'technical purposes,' limiting the scope of applicability of the main theorems.

The lower bound demonstrating action blow-up (Prop. 9) is proved only for a specific 1D two-component Gaussian mixture with equal variance; it is unclear how broadly this pessimistic result generalizes to higher dimensions or more general non-log-concave targets, so the motivation for Section 6 rests on a narrow example.

No lower bounds are given for the AIS/JE upper complexity bounds themselves (acknowledged as an open question by the authors), so the tightness of the claimed Oe(dβ²A²/ε⁴) rate is unverified, weakening the strength of the main claimed contribution.

The overall exposition is dense and highly technical with limited intuition-building for a broader ML audience; practical algorithmic guidance (e.g., how to choose or estimate A, how to select annealing schedules in practice) is thin, reducing the paper's accessibility and immediate impact.

strengths: Establishes the first non-asymptotic oracle complexity bound for Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) without requiring log-concavity or other isoperimetric assumptions on the target, extending prior analyses (e.g., Brosse et al., Ge et al.) that relied on such conditions.

Introduces a clean and elegant proof technique connecting the free-energy estimation error to the 'action' of the interpolating curve of measures (via Girsanov theorem and Wasserstein metric derivatives/optimal transport), giving a unifying lens for analyzing Jarzynski equality, AIS, and reverse-diffusion-based estimators.

Provides a rigorous non-asymptotic analysis of the Jarzynski equality/annealed Langevin diffusion (Thm. 6), filling a gap since prior JE analyses were largely asymptotic or restricted to simple work distributions.

Identifies and proves (Prop. 9) an exponential lower bound on the action of the standard geometric interpolation curve for a simple Gaussian mixture, giving concrete theoretical justification for why geometric tempering can be inefficient and motivating the proposed alternative.

Proposes a novel reverse-diffusion-sampler-based algorithm for normalizing constant estimation and establishes a framework (Thm. 11, Prop. 10) showing the OU-process curve has provably bounded action under mild conditions, contrasting nicely with the geometric-interpolation lower bound.

Extensive and careful appendix: discusses relation to thermodynamic integration (showing it is a special case of AIS with perfect kernels), reviews and critiques existing bias/variance-based guarantees, proves equivalence between complexity of estimating Z and F, and even revisits related learned-sampler methods (PIS, CMCD) with improved non-asymptotic guarantees derived from the same proof technique.

The complexity bounds are interpretable and connect to physical intuition (e.g., dissipated work, second law of thermodynamics), strengthening the conceptual contribution beyond a purely technical result.
weaknesses: No empirical validation: the paper is purely theoretical with no experiments illustrating or sanity-checking the derived complexity bounds (e.g., verifying the ε^-4 or action-dependent scaling on toy problems), which would help demonstrate practical relevance.

The core complexity bounds depend crucially on the action A of the curve, which the paper itself shows can be exponentially large in natural cases (Prop. 9); the proposed RDS-based remedy is only presented as a 'framework' whose end-to-end complexity relies on citing external results for score estimation, some of which are themselves exponential in dimension or problem parameters, so the practical benefit of Sec. 6 over AIS is not fully quantified.
No matching lower bounds are established, so the tightness of the derived upper complexity bounds (Thms. 6, 8, 11) remains open, as acknowledged by the authors themselves in the conclusion.

Several technical assumptions (e.g., R ≲ 1/√β for the stationary point, restrictions on the annealing schedule exponent r ≲ 1) are somewhat restrictive and their necessity/tightness is not deeply discussed.

The presentation is very dense and notation-heavy, which may limit accessibility to a broader audience despite the high technical quality; a running toy example throughout the main text (beyond the Gaussian mixture used only for the lower bound) could improve intuition.

The overall ε-dependence in the final bounds (e.g., ε^-4 for AIS) is quite pessimistic relative to what is empirically observed for AIS in practice, and the paper does not discuss how loose these bounds might be in typical use cases.

strengths: First rigorous non-asymptotic complexity analysis of Jarzynski Equality and Annealed Importance Sampling that does not rely on isoperimetric (e.g. log-concavity) assumptions on the target, filling a clear and long-standing gap between the widespread practical use of these methods and their theoretical understanding.

Technically sophisticated proof machinery combining Girsanov's theorem, forward/backward SDEs, and optimal-transport metric derivatives/action, presented with care (including careful handling of backward stochastic integrals and Nelson's relation) and extended from the sampling setting of Guo et al. (2025) to the conceptually distinct task of normalizing constant estimation.

The paper draws an interesting quantitative bridge between sampling complexity and normalizing-constant-estimation complexity in the continuous, non-log-concave setting, echoing (and refining) the classical discrete-setting equivalence of Jerrum et al. (1986).

Proposition 1 gives a compelling, rigorous explanation (exponential lower bound on the action) for the well-known but previously only qualitatively understood 'mass teleportation' failure mode of geometric interpolation/AIS on multimodal targets.

The proposed RDS-based normalizing constant estimator is a natural and well-motivated response to this identified weakness, with a general complexity framework (Thm. 5) that can incorporate several existing reverse-diffusion sampling algorithms (RDMC, RSDMC, ZODMC, SNDMC).

Extensive appendix with full proofs, useful supplementary lemmas (Girsanov corollaries, median trick, Rényi divergence variance bound), and additional discussion (e.g., TI as special case of AIS, comparisons with PIS/CMCD) substantially strengthen rigor and completeness.

Experiments, while modest in scale, clearly illustrate the qualitative phenomenon predicted by the theory: AIS/TI with geometric interpolation fail on multimodal targets while RDS-based methods succeed, providing empirical support for the theoretical narrative.
weaknesses: The central complexity bounds are expressed in terms of the curve's action A, which is itself generally intractable to compute or bound tightly for realistic non-log-concave targets; aside from the specific two-component Gaussian mixture example, there is little guidance on how large or small A typically is, limiting the practical interpretability of the main theorems (an issue the authors themselves acknowledge).

The complexity guarantees for the proposed RDS-based algorithm (Thm. 5) are essentially inherited from existing reverse-diffusion sampler analyses, most of which are exponential in dimension or other problem parameters (except SNDMC in fixed dimension); thus the paper does not establish a rigorous worst-case complexity advantage of RDS over AIS, only a favorable action bound (Prop. 2) and empirical evidence.

Experimental validation is limited to two 2-dimensional toy multimodal distributions; there is no empirical study of how the estimators scale with dimension, nor any real-world or higher-dimensional benchmark, making it hard to assess practical significance of the theory beyond the illustrative examples.

Tightness of the derived upper bounds (Thms. 2 and 4) is unknown, and the exponential action lower bound (Prop. 1) does not directly translate into a proven exponential lower bound on runtime for JE/AIS, leaving a gap between the negative result and its interpreted implication.

The two-phase AIS algorithm (TI for Z0 estimation, then AIS with a specific polynomial annealing schedule) and its complexity analysis are quite involved, and practical guidance for choosing r, T, or the schedule outside the theoretical construction is limited.

The paper is dense and highly technical, with the main text relying heavily on deferred proofs; some readers may find it hard to extract clear, actionable takeaways beyond the qualitative message that action matters and OU-based curves are preferable to geometric tempering.

strengths: Establishes the first non-asymptotic oracle complexity bounds for both the Jarzynski equality (continuous ALD) and annealed importance sampling (AIS) for normalizing constant estimation, without relying on isoperimetric assumptions (e.g., log-concavity, PI, LSI) on the target, which meaningfully extends prior work (Brosse et al. 2018; Ge et al. 2020) that was restricted to log-concave settings.

The technical machinery is rigorous and creative: it combines Girsanov's theorem, forward/backward SDE duality, and the Wasserstein action of a curve of measures to give clean, interpretable complexity bounds (Thms. 2 and 4), with detailed, mostly self-contained proofs in the appendix.

Proposition 1 gives a nice, non-trivial exponential lower bound on the action of the widely-used geometric interpolation for a simple bimodal Gaussian mixture, providing a rigorous, quantitative explanation of the well-known 'mass teleportation'/mode-switching phenomenon that was previously only understood empirically or qualitatively.

The paper draws an interesting parallel between sampling complexity (Guo et al. 2025) and normalizing-constant-estimation complexity, showing they share essentially the same action-dependent scaling, which is a conceptually appealing bridge between two closely related but distinct problems.

Motivated by the action-based diagnosis, the paper proposes an alternative curve based on the OU process/reverse diffusion samplers (RDS), proves the action along this curve is well-behaved under mild assumptions (Prop. 2), and builds a full complexity framework and estimator (Thm. 5) around it, backed by an empirical comparison against AIS/TI showing improved mode coverage and normalizing-constant accuracy on two toy multimodal problems.

The appendix is unusually thorough: it discusses the relation of the (1) accuracy criterion to bias/variance, equivalence of Z- and F- estimation complexity, an upper bound on JE's normalized variance via Rényi divergence, and connections to other learning-based samplers (PIS, CMCD), giving a well-rounded treatment of the estimation criterion and providing several supplementary technical results beyond the main text.
weaknesses: The headline complexity bounds are parameterized by the action A of the interpolation curve, which the paper itself shows can be exponentially large for even simple non-log-concave targets (Prop. 1); this substantially limits the practical value of Thms. 2 and 4, since for genuinely multimodal problems the 'improved' bounds are still vacuous/exponential, and the paper does not make this limitation sufficiently prominent outside the conclusion.

The proposed fix (RDS-based estimator) does not actually resolve the underlying hardness: the cited complexities for RDMC/RSDMC/ZODMC/SNDMC used to instantiate Thm. 5 are themselves exponential in d, β, or 1/ε in the worst case, so the paper trades one exponential dependency (action) for another (RDS score-estimation cost) without a clear net theoretical gain—this trade-off is acknowledged only qualitatively at the end of Sec. 5 rather than analyzed quantitatively.

No lower bounds are provided to assess tightness of the derived upper bounds (Thms. 2 and 4); the paper explicitly lists this as an open question, but for a complexity-focused paper the absence of any matching lower bound (even under stronger assumptions) is a significant gap.

Empirical validation is very limited: only two toy 2D distributions (a modified Müller-Brown potential and a 4-component Gaussian mixture) are used, with no experiments in even moderate dimension, no verification that the derived complexity scalings actually track the theory (e.g., no plots of error vs. predicted T, M, or dimension), and no comparison against other more competitive neural/learned samplers referenced in the related work (PIS, CMCD, NETS, etc.) that could serve as stronger baselines beyond vanilla AIS/TI.

The AIS analysis (Thm. 4) is derived under a fairly restrictive and specific parametric annealing schedule λ(θ)=2β(1-θ)^r with r essentially close to 1, and a particular discretization scheme (exponential integrator with one LMC step per transition); it is unclear how sensitive the results are to these choices or how they would extend to other common annealing schedules used in practice.

Some of the core proof strategies (action-based analysis of annealed dynamics via Girsanov/continuity equation) are adapted fairly directly from Guo et al. (2025), and while the extension to normalizing-constant estimation and the backward-SDE treatment are genuine additions, the degree of independent methodological novelty relative to that prior work could be viewed as incremental.

The practical interpretability of the 'action' as a diagnostic quantity is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be poorly understood, which weakens the paper's claim of providing practically actionable insight into why/when annealing works, beyond a purely mathematical characterization.

strengths: The paper provides the first non-asymptotic oracle complexity analysis for AIS without assuming log-concavity of the target, filling an important gap given AIS's widespread empirical use but limited theoretical understanding.

The core technical contribution—relating normalizing-constant estimation complexity to the 'action' of the interpolating curve via optimal transport and Girsanov-theorem-based forward/backward SDE analysis—is elegant and avoids explicit isoperimetric assumptions (e.g., log-Sobolev/Poincaré), a genuine advance over prior work (Brosse et al., Ge et al.) that required strong convexity/log-concavity.

The paper establishes a clean quantitative link between sampling complexity (Guo et al. 2025) and normalizing-constant-estimation complexity in continuous, non-log-concave settings, extending the classical discrete-case equivalence (Jerrum et al. 1986) to a new regime.

Proposition 1 gives a rigorous exponential lower bound on the action of the widely-used geometric interpolation for a simple bimodal target, providing a quantitative and novel explanation of the well-known 'mass teleportation' phenomenon.

Motivated by this limitation, the authors propose a principled alternative (reverse diffusion samplers) with a matching complexity framework (Thm. 5), backed by clear pseudocode (Algs. 1 and 2) and experiments showing RDS methods substantially outperform TI/AIS on multimodal targets.

The theoretical exposition is careful and thorough: extensive appendices with self-contained treatment of backward SDEs/Girsanov theorem, detailed proofs, discussion of bias/variance vs. the (1) criterion, and connections to stochastic thermodynamics (Jarzynski/Crooks).
The related work section is unusually thorough and situates the contribution well relative to equilibrium/non-equilibrium methods, isoperimetry-based analyses, and learning-based neural samplers.
weaknesses: Experimental validation is limited to two small 2D toy distributions (modified Müller-Brown and a 4-component Gaussian mixture); there is no demonstration at higher dimensions or on any realistic Bayesian/statistical-mechanics benchmark, limiting confidence in the practical significance of the proposed RDS-based algorithm at scale.

The overall complexity of the proposed RDS-based estimator inherits the often exponential-in-dimension complexity of existing score-estimation subroutines (RDMC, RSDMC, ZODMC, SNDMC), as acknowledged in App. E.5; the practical scalability advantage over AIS beyond low-dimensional experiments is unclear.

The authors acknowledge the tightness of the derived upper bounds (Thms. 2 and 4) is unknown, and that the action lower bound (Prop. 1) does not rigorously imply JE requires exponentially long time to converge, leaving a gap between the theoretical narrative and a fully rigorous complexity separation.

The practical interpretability of the 'action' quantity is admittedly not well understood, making it harder for practitioners to use the theory to design interpolation schedules in real applications beyond the specific cases analyzed.

The dense, highly technical exposition (heavy reliance on results deferred to a long appendix) may reduce accessibility; some steps (e.g., compensatory drift choice, static Schrödinger bridge duality) would benefit from more high-level intuition in the main text.
